NextItNet’s residual stacks of dilated causal convolutions expand the architectural receptive field; this does not guarantee that distant interactions materially influence predictions. For stride-one layers, calculate the receptive-field span as R = 1 + Σℓ(kℓ−1)dℓ, counting every temporal convolution. Compare that bound with measured sensitivity by lag to distinguish inaccessible history from accessible but weakly used history. [Original NextItNet paper](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf).

Recent evidence supports position-specific probes. An ECIR 2024 study found that removing recent training interactions hurt recommendation accuracy substantially more than removing early or middle interactions, and introduced finite rank-biased overlap (FRBO) for comparing finite recommendation lists. These are training-data perturbation results, so they do not directly establish the behavior of a frozen NextItNet under inference-time edits. A 2025 reproducibility study also emphasizes how preprocessing and experimental configuration affect conclusions. [Perturbation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13165), [reproducibility study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03873).

Practical diagnostic proposal: freeze each category’s single model and validation candidates; compare intact history, recent-only suffixes, older-only prefixes, and permutations of nonpadding items, including shuffles that preserve the last item. Report paired target-rank changes, ΔHR@10, top-10 overlap or FRBO, stratified by history length and receptive-field coverage. Separate deletion/repacking from position-preserving masking because repacking changes convolutional distances. In evaluation mode, verify final-nonpadding readout for left-padded histories—never count−1—and test that perturbations outside the computed receptive field leave scores unchanged for a purely local backbone. Treat these proposed probes as model-sensitivity measurements and stale-interest hypotheses, not causal evidence about user intent.
